newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: FOCUS-SLOVAK TRADE GAP SLOWDOWN TEMPORARY-ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-SLOVAK TRADE GAP SLOWDOWN TEMPORARY-ANALYSTS.

text.p: Growth in Slovakia's foreign trade deficit slowed in June but analysts said this was more a short-term phenomenon than a reversal of long-term negative developments.
The Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) said on Wednesday the trade gap widened to 32.57 billion crowns in the first half of 1997, from a 29.62 billion shortfall in the first five months.
Cumulative imports totalled 177.33 billion crowns, a year- on-year increase of 12.6 percent, while exports rose 12.9 percent, compared with the first half of last year to 144.76 billion crowns.
The trade gap for June alone was 2.95 billion crowns, down from 4.21 billion in May.
"The small deficit increase in June is better than was generally expected," said one foreign bank analyst.

"But it is certainly too early to celebrate any reversal of the trade trend, since the June slowdown was only a natural move after the rapid May deficit increase," the analyst said, adding the shortfall was likely to accelerate later in the year, especialy in the last quarter.
Analysts said they saw little room for any radical improvement of Slovakia's trade balance in coming months.

"I'm afraid the June figures do not indicate a longer- term improvement and there are several factors behind our expectations of a further widening of the trade deficit," said ING Barings' analyst Martin Barto.
An expected slowdown in industrial output due to summer holidays and high interest rates are the main factors expected to prevent any radical growth in exports.
On the other hand, a large portion of unavoidable imports, such as of raw materials, will prevent major cuts in imports.
Fossil fuels and mineral oils accounted for the largest part of imported goods, totalling 31.22 billion crowns, a 17.9 percent year-on-year increase.

Technology imports, mainly equipment for upgrading of the ageing Jaslovske Bohunice nuclear power plant and the completion of the Mochovce nuclear plant, totalled 28.29 billion crowns, up 20.2 percent year-on-year.
"The country will have to continue buying oil and gas abroad and it will also have to keep up quite large technology imports for the Mochovce plant and the GSM network," said Barto.
The first block of the Mochovce plant should be completed by June 1998 and the second by March 1999.

"The world FX market development will also influence Slovakia's trade balance, since a large portion of imports is paid for in dollars, but we think the full year deficit will probably be higher than official forecasts," Barto said.
The government has said the 1997 trade gap should not exceed last year's shortfall of around 65 billion crowns.
"I would say the full year figure will be above 70 billion crowns, maybe around 75 billion," the foreign analyst said.
Economists said the widening of the deficit, though slower than expected, also removed any chances for the central bank (NBS) to ease monetary policy.
The NBS considers the development of foreign trade as one of the main factors for assessment of future monetary policy.
Since summer 1996, the NBS has been running a tight policy in order to curb consumer-oriented credit expansion which was fuelling growth in imports.
The NBS, in the face of pressure on the crown, moved further some two months ago and radicaly squeezed crown market liquidity. This pushed interbank rates above 20 percent.
"The NBS is not likely to ease its policy in the near future since its ful- year target of five percent of GDP seems unreachable," Barto said.
-- Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-521-8402
